input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-471: Professional Communications. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course focuses on developing and improving verbal and written communication skills specific to the discipline of computer science. Topics include the different forms of writing in computer science (books, theses, journal articles, technical reports, manuscripts, etc.), writing styles of computer scientists, document readability and usability, documents for career readiness, effective presentations, teamwork and peer review, research methods, experimentation, documenting mathematics and algorithms, proper formatting of graphs, figures, and tables, and ethical, social, and professional issues facing Computer Scientists. This course is approved as Writing Intensive. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-472. This class is restricted to students with at least 4th year standing COMPSCI-BS or COMPSCI-2M Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: Writing Intensive: Program Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[mit-algorithms]
Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

[opendsa]
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.

[rit-csci-471]
This course focuses on developing and improving verbal and written communication skills specific to the discipline of computer science. Topics include the different forms of writing in computer science (books, theses, journal articles, technical reports, manuscripts, etc.), writing styles of computer scientists, document readability and usability, documents for career readiness, effective presentations, teamwork and peer review, research methods, experimentation, documenting mathematics and algorithms, proper formatting of graphs, figures, and tables, and ethical, social, and professional issues facing Computer Scientists. This course is approved as Writing Intensive. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-472. This class is restricted to students with at least 4th year standing COMPSCI-BS or COMPSCI-2M Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: Writing Intensive: Program Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: CSCI-471 is a Writing Intensive course restricted to fourth-year COMPSCI-BS or COMPSCI-2M students and focuses on discipline-specific communication skills.
beats.example: A senior software engineer preparing a technical report for a research grant must follow this course's formatting and ethical guidelines.
beats.title: Course Scope & Audience
beats.visualDirection: Display a course catalog excerpt highlighting the Writing Intensive designation, fourth-year restriction, and lecture contact hours.

beats.claim: Computer science communication utilizes distinct document forms such as books, theses, journal articles, technical reports, and manuscripts, each with specific structural and tonal
beats.example: A thesis requires a comprehensive literature review and methodology section, whereas a journal article emphasizes novel findings and concise results.
beats.title: Document Types in Computer Science
beats.visualDirection: Show a comparison chart listing document types alongside their primary purposes and typical audience expectations.

beats.claim: Documenting mathematics and algorithms requires precise input/output specifications, correctness proofs, and resource bound analysis to ensure reproducibility.
beats.example: A developer documenting a sorting algorithm must explicitly state preconditions, postconditions, and time complexity before presenting pseudocode.
beats.title: Algorithm Documentation Standards
beats.visualDirection: Display a template for algorithm documentation with labeled sections for inputs, outputs, correctness arguments, and asymptotic analysis.

beats.claim: Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size, enabling accurate comparisons of algorithm efficiency across different problem scales.
beats.example: Using Big-O notation, a developer can demonstrate that a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm outperforms a linear scan for large datasets.
beats.title: Asymptotic Notation & Resource Bounds
beats.visualDirection: Graph input size against resource consumption using logarithmic scales to illustrate linear, logarithmic, and polynomial growth patterns.

beats.claim: Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible, directly impacting document clarity and usability.
beats.example: Selecting a hash table over a linked list for key-value storage reduces lookup time from O(n) to O(1) on average, which must be explicitly noted in technical documentation.
beats.title: Data Structure Representation Choices
beats.visualDirection: Show side-by-side diagrams of a hash table and a linked list with annotated operation costs and collision handling strategies.

beats.claim: Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions, requiring clear visual and textual explanations.
beats.example: A network engineer documenting a shortest path algorithm must explain how adjacency matrices or adjacency lists represent the graph structure.
beats.title: Graph Algorithms & Traversal
beats.visualDirection: Render a directed graph with labeled vertices and edges, highlighting traversal paths and connectivity metrics.

beats.claim: Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems, improving efficiency by avoiding redundant computations in complex algorithmic documentation.
beats.example: A developer documenting a Fibonacci sequence calculator must show how memoization tables store intermediate results to reduce time complexity.
beats.title: Dynamic Programming & Overlapping Subproblems
beats.visualDirection: Display a memoization table filling process with arrows indicating subproblem reuse and final solution assembly.

beats.claim: Proper formatting of graphs, figures, and tables ensures document readability and usability, preventing misinterpretation of technical data.
beats.example: A bar chart comparing algorithm runtimes must include axis labels, a legend, and consistent units to accurately convey performance differences.
beats.title: Visual Data Formatting
beats.visualDirection: Show a before-and-after comparison of a poorly formatted chart versus a professionally formatted technical figure with clear axes and legends.

beats.claim: Teamwork and peer review are essential professional communication practices that improve document quality through structured feedback and collaborative refinement.
beats.example: A research group uses a standardized peer review checklist to evaluate algorithm correctness, clarity of notation, and adherence to formatting standards before submission.
beats.title: Teamwork & Peer Review Practices
beats.visualDirection: Display a peer review checklist template with categories for correctness, readability, formatting, and ethical compliance.

beats.claim: Ethical, social, and professional issues facing Computer Scientists require transparent communication, proper attribution, and responsible handling of research data.
beats.example: A developer documenting a machine learning model must disclose training data sources, potential biases, and limitations to maintain professional integrity.
beats.title: Ethical & Professional Considerations
beats.visualDirection: Show a professional communication checklist highlighting ethical disclosure, authorship attribution, and data privacy compliance.

learningObjectives: Define and distinguish between the primary document types used in computer science research and industry.
Apply standard formatting and readability principles to technical documents and visual data representations.
Evaluate ethical and professional considerations in computer science communication and peer review processes.
